kurals.tamil:
நாநலம் என்னும் நலனுடைமை அந்நலம்
யாநலத்து உள்ளதூஉம் அன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Naanalam ennum nalanudaimai annalam
Yaanalaththu ulladhooum andru.
kurals.meaning: The gift called goodness of the tongue is a wealth in its own right; it is not merely one item among the other good things a person may possess.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a treasure box holding gold, toys and books. A kind, clear way of speaking is not just one more thing in the box; it is like a special key that opens many other boxes. This kural says being able to speak well is a treasure all by itself.
kurals.university: The chapter opens the minister’s second great qualification after the preceding chapter on the minister (அமைச்சு, ch. 64): nā-nalam, literally “tongue-goodness”, is framed as a nalan-uṭaimai, a possession or wealth in the same grammatical mould as kalvi-uṭaimai or aṟivu-uṭaimai elsewhere in the text. The second line, yā-nalattu uḷḷatūum anṟu, says this good is “not contained within any other good”; the lengthened form uḷḷatūum is an alapeṭai (metrical prolongation). Parimelazhagar explains that eloquence is a distinct excellence because the other goods of a minister (lineage, learning, wealth) cannot be made effective in council without it, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow this reading of it as a unique, self-standing merit. Some later commentators, including Kalaignar, read the line more strongly as “the best of all wealth”, a slight shift from “not included among” to “superior to” the other goods. The text is stable across ytamizh.com and the older sandhi-joined edition at thirukkural-thamizh.org (நாநல மென்னு நலனுடைமை யந்நலம்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Vak Sukta of the Rigveda, Vāk (divine Speech) speaks of herself as a queen and gatherer of treasures, the power who makes the one she loves mighty, a seer and a sage.
hinduism.explanation: The hymn treats Speech not as a tool but as a sovereign goddess who holds wealth and gives greatness to those she favours; later tradition connects her with Sarasvatī.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the hymn counts speech itself as a treasure, not an accessory to other treasures.
hinduism.source: Rigveda 10.125 (Vak Sukta), trans. R. T. H. Griffith
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match on speech as a form of wealth; the Vedic hymn is cosmological rather than about a minister’s skill.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The officers answered, Never man spake like this man.”
christianity.explanation: Temple officers sent to arrest Jesus return empty-handed, giving as their only excuse the unmatched quality of his speech.
christianity.tie_back: The officers treat Jesus’ speech as a power in a class of its own, which is what the Kural means by a good not contained in other goods.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good fit on unique excellence of speech, though the Gospel stresses divine authority rather than acquired skill.

islam.explanation: Surah ar-Rahman lists al-bayān (clear, articulate expression) among God’s first gifts to humankind, right after creating the human being and teaching the Qur’an.
islam.tie_back: The Qur’an counts clear speech as a distinct divine gift, much as the Kural counts nā-nalam as its own kind of wealth.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match: bayān is eloquence as a gift in its own right.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A word fitly spoken Is like apples of gold in settings of silver.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb compares a well-placed word to a precious object set in precious metal, a thing of both value and beauty.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts describe good speech as treasure, with value apart from the speaker’s other goods.
judaism._accuracy_note: Direct image of speech as wealth; Proverbs stresses timeliness slightly more than the Kural does here.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Anguttara Nikaya’s list of pre-eminent disciples, the Buddha names the monk Vangīsa as foremost among those gifted with ready, inspired speech (paṭibhāna).
buddhism.explanation: Eloquence is recognised as a separate excellence worth naming, alongside wisdom, psychic power and other distinctions.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural also treats eloquence as its own distinct merit, not something absorbed into other virtues.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Supports speech as a distinct excellence; the Buddhist list is a record of monks, not a teaching about statecraft.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hermes, messenger of the gods, was honoured as Hermes Logios, patron of eloquence and persuasive speech, and the Homeric Hymn to Hermes shows the infant god talking his way out of trouble before Zeus.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Greeks gave eloquence its own divine patron, separate from the gods of war, wealth or wisdom.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Giving eloquence its own god reflects the Kural’s view that speech is a good in its own category.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Reasonable parallel; the hymn celebrates Hermes’ cunning more than disciplined, ethical oratory.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Nicocles, Isocrates delivers his famous praise of logos: speech is what raises humans above animals, lets them found cities, make laws and invent arts, and good speech is the outward sign of a sound mind.
philosophy.explanation: Isocrates argues that the capacity for speech is the source of nearly every civilised good.
philosophy.tie_back: Isocrates, like Valluvar, ranks eloquence as a good of its own order rather than one virtue among many.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong parallel on the unique rank of speech; Isocrates speaks of human speech in general, not only a counsellor’s.

kurals.tamil:
ஆக்கமுங் கேடும் அதனால் வருதலால்
காத்தோம்பல் சொல்லின்கட் சோர்வு.
kurals.transliteration:
Aakkamung kedum adhanaal varudhalaal
Kaaththombal sollinkat sorvu.
kurals.meaning: Since both prosperity and ruin come through speech, a person must guard carefully against any slip in what they say.
kurals.elementary: Words are like the steering wheel of a car: turn it well and you get home safely, jerk it carelessly and you crash. Because words can build things up or break them down, we should be careful never to say the wrong thing.
kurals.university: Ākkam (growth, prosperity) and kēṭu (ruin) are the paired outcomes that Valluvar often sets against each other, and here both are said to arrive “by it” (atanāl), meaning speech. The verb phrase kāttu ōmpal, “guarding and protecting”, is a doubled imperative of care, and cōrvu names a lapse, slip or momentary negligence, not deliberate lying. Parimelazhagar reads the couplet as advice to the minister, whose words in council can raise or ruin the king’s affairs, and so the lapse to be guarded against is any fault in word choice or timing. Modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Kalaignar) widen it into a universal maxim of verbal care. The older edition prints the first line in sandhi form (ஆக்கமுங் கேடு மதனால் வருதலாற்), with no difference in meaning.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Udyoga Parva, Vidura warns Dhritarashtra that wounds from arrows and axes heal, but wounds from harsh words do not, and that a wise person never lets such arrows of speech fly.
hinduism.explanation: Vidura’s political counsel treats careless speech as a direct cause of lasting enmity and ruin in a royal household.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Vidura tells a ruler’s counsellor to guard every word because ruin can come from speech.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Vidura Niti), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good fit on speech causing ruin; paraphrased from memory of the Vidura Niti, so the exact section number is not given.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that a person’s words decide their standing, for good or ill.
christianity.tie_back: Words bring either justification or condemnation, just as the Kural says they bring either gain or ruin.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close in structure: one source, two opposite outcomes.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice.”
islam.explanation: The verse commands qawlan sadīdan, straight and well-aimed speech, and the next verse promises that God will then set right the believers’ deeds.
islam.tie_back: The Qur’an ties good outcomes to carefully aimed speech, as the Kural ties prosperity to guarding one’s words.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on careful speech leading to good results; the Qur’anic frame is moral and religious rather than political.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs 18:21 teaches that death and life are in the power of the tongue, and that those who love it will eat its fruit.
judaism.explanation: The sage says the tongue decides between life and death, and people reap the results of how they use it.
judaism.tie_back: Death and life in Proverbs, like ruin and gain in the Kural, both come through speech.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; paraphrased because the JPS wording was not checked for this verse.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kokālika Sutta the Buddha says that a person is born with an axe in the mouth, with which the fool cuts himself when he speaks wrongly.
buddhism.explanation: The monk Kokālika slanders the chief disciples and suffers terribly for it; the verses warn that reckless words wound the speaker most of all.
buddhism.tie_back: The axe in the mouth is a vivid picture of the Kural’s warning that ruin can come through one’s own careless speech.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on the ruin side; the sutta concerns slander more than general care in speech.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Niobe publicly boasts that her many children make her greater than the goddess Leto, and in response Apollo and Artemis kill her children one by one.
greek_mythology.explanation: A single proud speech in front of the people of Thebes brings total ruin on her household.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Niobe’s story shows the ruin side of the Kural: one slip of the tongue destroys everything.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good as a cautionary tale; the myth is about hubris toward the gods, not the craft of speech.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Encomium of Helen, Gorgias calls speech a mighty lord that with a tiny body does divine works, and compares its effect on the soul to drugs on the body: some cure, some kill.
philosophy.explanation: Gorgias argues that speech can bring either healing or harm, depending on how it is used.
philosophy.tie_back: Speech as both cure and poison is Gorgias’ version of the Kural’s gain and ruin.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close on speech as a double-edged power; Gorgias is making a rhetorical display, not giving moral advice.

kurals.tamil:
கேட்டார்ப் பிணிக்கும் தகையவாய்க் கேளாரும்
வேட்ப மொழிவதாம் சொல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kettaarp pinikkum thakaiyavaaik kelaarum
Vetpa mozhivadhaam sol.
kurals.meaning: True eloquence holds those who hear it as if bound, and is spoken so well that even those who have not heard it long to hear it.
kurals.elementary: Think of a storyteller so good that the children listening can’t look away, and children walking past stop and want to join in. That is what this kural calls real speaking skill.
kurals.university: The key verb piṇittal means to bind or tie (as with a rope), so the listener is pictured as captured by the speech, and vēṭpa means “so as to make them desire”. The contrast kēṭṭār / kēḷār, “those who have heard / those who have not heard”, is read two ways. Parimelazhagar takes kēṭṭār as allies or friends (those already listening) and kēḷār as enemies or those who refuse to listen; this is why Pope’s gloss speaks of binding friends and making even enemies desire. Solomon Pappaiah follows this reading but also records the plainer sense of those who heard before and those who have not yet heard. The couplet is effectively the chapter’s definition of sol-vanmai, ending emphatically with -ām col, “that is speech”.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Hanuman first meets Rama and Lakshmana in the Kishkindha Kanda, Rama praises his speech as faultless, well-ordered and pleasing, saying that such words could win over even an enemy with his sword raised.
hinduism.explanation: Rama sees Hanuman’s grammar, tone and order as signs of a learned envoy whose words would charm any listener.
hinduism.tie_back: An enemy won over by speech is the Kural’s picture of even unwilling hearers longing to listen.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Excellent thematic match, fitting Parimelazhagar’s friends and enemies reading; paraphrased, not quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And all bare him witness, and wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth.”
christianity.explanation: In the synagogue at Nazareth the whole audience is held by the grace of Jesus’ words, even those who were sceptical of him.
christianity.tie_back: Listeners held in wonder are what the Kural means by speech that binds those who hear it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good on the captivating effect; the same scene soon turns hostile, which the Kural does not imagine.

islam.quote_or_event: “Some eloquent speech has the influence of magic.”
islam.explanation: After two men from the east gave speeches, the Prophet remarked on how eloquence can move people like a spell, even changing the minds of those who had refused.
islam.tie_back: The hadith’s magic-like hold on listeners is the Kural’s power to bind hearers.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on the binding power of eloquence; the hadith is often read as a mild caution as well as praise.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ecclesiastes says the Preacher sought out pleasing words and wrote truth rightly, and that the words of the wise are like goads and firmly fixed nails.
judaism.explanation: Kohelet joins pleasing form with true content, speech that both attracts and holds fast in the mind.
judaism.tie_back: Words that please and stick like nails match speech that draws people in and holds them.
judaism._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit; paraphrased, and the focus is on written wisdom as much as speech.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Brahmāyu Sutta describes the Buddha’s voice as having eight qualities, among them being clear, intelligible, sweet, audible and resonant, so that it reaches the whole assembly and no further.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist texts treat the Buddha’s speech as naturally absorbing to every listener in the assembly.
buddhism.tie_back: A voice made to reach and hold every listener fits the Kural’s ideal of speech that binds its hearers.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Supports the theme of captivating speech; the sutta describes the voice’s qualities, not persuasion of unwilling hearers.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Orpheus sings before Hades and Persephone, and his song so enthrals the underworld that the shades weep and the rulers of the dead, who never yield, grant his request.
greek_mythology.explanation: Even the powers most unwilling to listen are captured by Orpheus’ art.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Orpheus moving the unmoved matches the Kural’s speech that makes even those who would not listen long to hear.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Vivid parallel on binding listeners; Orpheus’ power is music, not oratory.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In De Oratore, Crassus says nothing seems finer than the power to hold assemblies by speech, win their minds, and move their wills wherever the speaker wishes.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero places the orator’s power to capture an audience at the centre of civic life.
philosophy.tie_back: Holding an assembly and winning its mind is exactly the binding power the Kural describes.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close match; paraphrased from the passage.

kurals.tamil:
திறனறிந்து சொல்லுக சொல்லை அறனும்
பொருளும் அதனினூஉங்கு இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thiranarindhu solluka sollai aranum
Porulum adhaninoongu il.
kurals.meaning: Speak only after understanding the nature of your listeners; there is no virtue or gain greater than speech fitted to its hearers.
kurals.elementary: You explain a game differently to your little cousin than to your teacher. This kural says the smart thing is to know who is listening and choose your words for them, and that doing this is one of the best things you can do.
kurals.university: Tiṟan aṟintu, “knowing the tiṟan”, is the interpretive crux. Parimelazhagar takes tiṟan as the qualities of the audience, and Solomon Pappaiah lists them: birth, learning, conduct, wealth, appearance and age. Mu. Varadarasanar reads tiṟan as the right manner or force of the words themselves, and Kalaignar as the underlying reason for speaking. The second line makes a striking claim with the comparative atanin ūungu, “beyond that”, lengthened for metre: neither aṟam (virtue, the first puruṣārtha) nor poruḷ (wealth, the second) exceeds well-fitted speech. The claim makes sense within Porutpal, where the minister’s speech is the means by which both dharma and wealth are secured for the kingdom.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking truthfully and beneficially and in avoiding speech that offends.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna defines disciplined speech as words that are true, pleasant and beneficial and do not upset the listener.
hinduism.tie_back: Speech shaped to benefit and not agitate the hearer requires the attention to the listener that the Kural demands.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Partial match: the Gita stresses ethical quality of speech more than tailoring it to the particular listener.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Colossians to speak graciously and fittingly so that they can answer each person appropriately.
christianity.tie_back: Knowing how to answer every person is the Kural’s tiṟan aṟintu, knowing the listener before speaking.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on fitting speech to each hearer.

islam.quote_or_event: “Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a way that is best.”
islam.explanation: The verse sets out graded forms of speech (wisdom, good exhortation, gracious argument), which exegetes relate to different kinds of listeners.
islam.tie_back: Choosing among wisdom, exhortation and argument according to the audience is the discernment the Kural asks for.
islam._accuracy_note: Good fit; the audience-matching reading comes from classical tafsir rather than the verse’s wording.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmudic principle that the Torah speaks in the language of human beings (dibbra Torah ki-lshon benei adam) holds that even divine teaching is expressed in forms its hearers can grasp.
judaism.explanation: The rabbis explain the Torah’s ordinary phrasing as God fitting speech to the human audience.
judaism.tie_back: If even revelation adapts to its listeners, the Kural’s advice to know the hearer before speaking has deep support.
judaism._accuracy_note: Next-best match: a principle of interpretation, not direct advice on oratory.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It is spoken at the right time. It is spoken in truth. It is spoken affectionately. It is spoken beneficially. It is spoken with a mind of good-will.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists five factors that make a statement well-spoken and blameless before the wise.
buddhism.tie_back: Right time and benefit to the listener depend on knowing one’s audience, which is the Kural’s point.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.198 (Vaca Sutta), trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on fitting speech to circumstance; the Kural’s claim that such speech exceeds virtue has no Buddhist equivalent.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the Greek army rushes for the ships in Iliad 2, Odysseus turns them back by speaking gently and respectfully to each chieftain but sharply to common soldiers, fitting his words to each listener.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus rescues the expedition by changing how he speaks according to the rank and mood of each person.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is a narrative example of the Kural’s rule: know the listener, then speak.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Clear narrative parallel; Odysseus’ rough treatment of commoners reflects Homeric hierarchy, not Valluvar’s ethics.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedrus, Socrates says a true art of speech must know the kinds of souls and the kinds of speeches, and fit each speech to the soul that will be moved by it.
philosophy.explanation: Plato makes knowledge of the audience the foundation of any real rhetoric.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato’s matching of speech to soul is almost exactly the Kural’s tiṟan aṟintu.

kurals.tamil:
சொல்லுக சொல்லைப் பிறிதோர்சொல் அச்சொல்லை
வெல்லுஞ்சொல் இன்மை அறிந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Solluka sollaip pirithorsol achchollai
Vellunjol inmai arindhu.
kurals.meaning: Speak your word only after making sure there is no other word that could defeat it.
kurals.elementary: Before you give your answer in a debate, check it from every side, like testing a bridge before you walk on it. If nobody can knock it down, then say it.
kurals.university: The couplet is famous for its sound play: col (word) appears five times in two lines, in collu-ka, collai, piṟitōr col, accollai and vellum col, so the verse enacts the verbal skill it recommends. The sense is that before speaking one should know (aṟintu) that no other word (piṟitu ōr col) that would overcome (vellum) that word exists (inmai). Parimelazhagar applies this to the minister in council, whose proposal must be answer-proof before it is offered to the king; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar say the same. The older edition shows sandhi forms (பிறிதோர்சொ லச்சொல்லை / வெல்லுஞ்சொ லின்மை யறிந்து), with no difference in meaning.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At King Janaka’s great debate, the sage Yajnavalkya answers challenger after challenger (Ashvala, Artabhaga, Gargi, Uddalaka and others) until none can refute him, and Gargi declares that no one will defeat him in argument about Brahman.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad presents Yajnavalkya’s answers as so exact that every counter-argument fails.
hinduism.tie_back: Speech that no other speech can defeat is exactly what Yajnavalkya shows in Janaka’s court.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel; the subject is metaphysics, not policy advice.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus promises his disciples that when they are put on trial they will be given words their opponents cannot answer.
christianity.tie_back: Words no adversary can gainsay are the Kural’s speech that no other word can overcome.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close in outcome; the Gospel credits divine gift rather than the speaker’s own preparation.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We strengthened his kingdom and gave him wisdom and discernment in speech.”
islam.explanation: David is given faṣl al-khiṭāb, which exegetes understand as decisive, conclusive speech that settles a matter.
islam.tie_back: Decisive speech that ends dispute is the Kural’s speech that cannot be defeated.
islam._accuracy_note: Good fit, and notably also set in a royal context.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Eleazar teaches in Pirkei Avot to be diligent in study and to know what to answer an unbeliever (apikoros).
judaism.explanation: The sage urges preparing answers in advance so that one’s reply to a challenger is sound.
judaism.tie_back: Preparing a reply that will hold against challenge is the discipline the Kural asks for before speaking.
judaism._accuracy_note: Fair match on preparing answers; narrower in scope. Some editions number this 2:19.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The debater Saccaka boasts that no one could face him in debate without trembling, but when he challenges the Buddha his own theses are refuted, and he is left silent and sweating before the assembly.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta contrasts a boastful debater with the Buddha, whose carefully built answers cannot be overturned.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha’s unanswerable replies show the kind of speech the Kural means; Saccaka shows what happens without it.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Achilles dies, Ajax and Ulysses (Odysseus) compete by speech for his armour before the Greek chiefs, and Ulysses’ carefully built argument defeats Ajax’s appeal to his strength.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid’s retelling, the armour goes to the man whose speech the council cannot answer.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ulysses wins because no counter-speech could overcome his, the Kural’s test for speaking.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good fit; Ovid leaves open whether Ulysses’ victory was just.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that the rhetorician must be able to argue both sides of a question, not to argue for the worse, but so that he can see how things stand and refute anyone who argues unfairly.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, good rhetoric means anticipating every counter-argument.
philosophy.tie_back: Knowing the opposing case in advance is how one makes sure that no word can defeat one’s own.

kurals.tamil:
வேட்பத்தாஞ் சொல்லிப் பிறர்சொல் பயன்கோடல்
மாட்சியின் மாசற்றார் கோள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vetpaththaanj sollip pirarsol payankodal
Maatchiyin maasatraar kol.
kurals.meaning: To speak so that others long to hear, and to take the useful meaning from what others say, is the practice of people of flawless excellence.
kurals.elementary: A good friend talks in a way you enjoy hearing, and when you talk, they listen for what you really mean instead of picking on small mistakes. This kural says the best people do both: speak well and listen well.
kurals.university: The couplet balances two actions: vēṭpat tām colli (oneself speaking so as to be desired) and piṟar col payan kōṭal (taking the payan, the fruit or meaning, of others’ words). Parimelazhagar adds that in hearing others one should grasp the substance while overlooking faults in their wording, and Solomon Pappaiah follows him. Māṭciyin mācaṟṟār, “those without stain in their excellence”, and kōḷ, “principle or settled practice”, present this as the rule of the most accomplished counsellors. It widens sol-vanmai from speaking to include skilled listening. The older edition reads பிறர்சொற் பயன்கோடன் in sandhi form.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Sanskrit tradition praises the haṃsa (swan) for its legendary ability to separate milk from water, and uses the haṃsa-kṣīra-nyāya as a maxim for taking the essence of what one hears and leaving the rest.
hinduism.explanation: The swan is the model of a discerning listener who keeps the worth in others’ words and lets the rest go.
hinduism.tie_back: Taking the fruit of others’ speech while ignoring its faults is the swan’s skill applied to listening.
hinduism.source: Haṃsa-kṣīra-nyāya (Sanskrit maxim), as collected in Wisdom Library
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good fit for the listening half; the maxim does not address pleasing speech.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.”
christianity.explanation: James puts eager listening before speech as the mark of a mature believer.
christianity.tie_back: Being swift to hear matches the Kural’s call to draw the meaning from others’ words.
christianity._accuracy_note: Covers the listening half well; says little about speaking so as to be desired.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who listen to speech and follow the best of it. Those are the ones Allah has guided, and those are people of understanding.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who hear what is said and take up the best of it.
islam.tie_back: Following the best of what one hears is almost the Kural’s piṟar col payan kōṭal.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close on the listening half of the couplet.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A wise man does not speak before one who is greater than he in wisdom, And does not break into his fellow’s speech; And is not hasty to answer; He asks what is relevant, and he answers to the point.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah lists the habits of a sage, which combine patient listening with relevant, well-aimed speech.
judaism.tie_back: Listening without interrupting and answering to the point is the double skill the Kural credits to the flawless.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on combined speaking and listening discipline.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “That monk who has control over his tongue, is moderate in speech, unassuming and who explains the Teaching in both letter and spirit — whatever he says is pleasing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada describes a monk whose restrained, clear speech is welcome to all who hear him.
buddhism.tie_back: Speech that is pleasing because of its restraint and meaning matches the first half of the Kural.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Fits the pleasing-speech half; does not address listening.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus pauses his tale of wanderings at the Phaeacian court, King Alcinous praises how gracefully and wisely he tells it, like a skilled bard, and begs him to keep going through the night.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus speaks so well that his hosts want more, and he in turn has listened carefully to their customs and wishes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A hearer begging for more is exactly vēṭpa, speech that makes people want to hear.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on the first half; the listening half is only implied.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his essay On Listening, Plutarch advises the young to listen to lectures by looking past a speaker’s style and faults of diction to take hold of what is useful, like a bee drawing honey.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch treats good listening as a skill: taking the benefit and ignoring the flaws.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly Parimelazhagar’s gloss: take the fruit of others’ words, overlook their faults.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, De recta ratione audiendi (On Listening)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close on the listening half; paraphrased.

kurals.tamil:
சொலல்வல்லன் சோர்விலன் அஞ்சான் அவனை
இகல்வெல்லல் யார்க்கும் அரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Solalvallan sorvilan anjaan avanai
Ikalvellal yaarkkum aridhu.
kurals.meaning: No one can easily overcome in contest a person who speaks with power, never slips, and does not fear.
kurals.elementary: Picture a class debate. The student who explains clearly, doesn’t forget their points, and isn’t scared to speak up is very hard to beat. This kural says those three things together make someone almost unbeatable.
kurals.university: Three predicate nouns build the ideal speaker: colal vallan (strong in speaking), cōrvilan (without lapse; Parimelazhagar glosses cōrvu as forgetfulness of what is to be said, echoing 642) and añcān (one who does not fear, above all fear of the assembly, the theme of chapter 73, Avaiyañcāmai). Ikal means enmity, rivalry or contention, so ikal vellal is victory through opposition; Pope renders it as intrigue or “hostile power”. Solomon Pappaiah expands the three terms to the ability to make others accept one’s thought, persistence even when the message is hard, and fearlessness even before hostile hearers. The older edition prints சோர்வில னஞ்சா னவனை / யிகல்வெல்லல் in sandhi form.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Before the Kurukshetra war, Krishna goes alone as envoy to the Kaurava court and argues the Pandavas’ case fearlessly and without faltering before Duryodhana and the assembled elders, who cannot answer him even though they reject him.
hinduism.explanation: The peace embassy shows the ideal envoy: articulate, unflinching and not intimidated by a hostile court.
hinduism.tie_back: Krishna has all three of the Kural’s qualities: power of speech, no lapse, and no fear.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Bhagavad-yana), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative fit; the embassy fails to prevent war, so being unbeatable in argument did not bring political success.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake.”
christianity.explanation: Stephen’s opponents in the synagogues cannot stand against his words, though they later have him killed.
christianity.tie_back: Stephen is the Kural’s speaker whom no one can overcome in open argument.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match; Stephen’s opponents turn to force, not words.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Allah] said, “Fear not. Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see.””
islam.explanation: Sent to confront Pharaoh, Moses and Aaron admit their fear, and God tells them to go without fear and speak.
islam.tie_back: Freedom from fear before a hostile power is the añcān (fearless) quality in the Kural’s portrait.
islam._accuracy_note: Covers fearlessness well, but only one of the three qualities.

judaism.quote_or_event: The prophet Nathan confronts King David over Bathsheba with a parable about a rich man who takes a poor man’s only lamb, leading David to condemn himself before Nathan says, “You are the man.”
judaism.explanation: Nathan speaks fearlessly to a king, and his carefully built story leaves David with no defence.
judaism.tie_back: Skill, precision and courage together make Nathan’s speech unanswerable, as the Kural describes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Prince Abhaya is sent by the Jain leader Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta with a two-horned question meant to trap the Buddha, but the Buddha answers calmly and exactly, and the trap fails.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta shows the Buddha as a speaker who cannot be cornered because he is clear, careful and unafraid.
buddhism.tie_back: A speaker no trap can catch fits the Kural’s ideal of one whom no rival can overcome.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “but when he raised his voice, and the words came driving from his deep chest like winter snow before the wind, then there was none to touch him”
greek_mythology.explanation: Antenor recalls Odysseus’ embassy to Troy: unimpressive at first sight, but when he spoke no one could match him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: “None to touch him” is the Homeric version of the Kural’s “hard for anyone to defeat”.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Excellent match, also set in a diplomatic embassy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Quintilian defines the ideal orator, following Cato, as a good man skilled in speaking (vir bonus dicendi peritus), who combines moral steadiness and courage with eloquence.
philosophy.explanation: For Quintilian, eloquence without character and courage is not true oratory.
philosophy.tie_back: Quintilian’s combination of skill, integrity and courage reflects the three qualities of the Kural.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good overlap; Quintilian stresses virtue more than invincibility.

kurals.tamil:
விரைந்து தொழில்கேட்கும் ஞாலம் நிரந்தினிது
சொல்லுதல் வல்லார்ப் பெறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Viraindhu thozhilkekkum gnaalam nirandhinidhu
Solludhal vallaarp perin.
kurals.meaning: If the world finds people who can speak in good order and pleasantly, it will quickly do what they ask.
kurals.elementary: If a coach explains the plan step by step and in a friendly way, the whole team gets moving straight away. This kural says people are happy to follow someone whose words are clear, well arranged and kind.
kurals.university: Nirantu, “in proper sequence, arranged in order”, is the key technical term: it describes dispositio, the arrangement of points in the right order, joined with initu, pleasantly. Toḻil kēṭkum ñālam, “the world that hears or obeys the command”, uses kēḷ in the sense of obedience, and viraintu (swiftly) stresses how quickly the result follows. Parimelazhagar reads ñālam as the people of the world and the couplet as describing the minister whose orderly, sweet speech gets the king’s business done at once. Pope’s rendering, the world gathering round, softens the sense of obedience. The older edition prints கேட்கு ஞால நிரந்தினிது.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Rigvedic hymn to Knowledge says that when the wise fashioned speech with their minds, sifting it as grain is cleaned with a sieve, friends recognised friendship and a blessed mark was set upon their speech.
hinduism.explanation: The hymn pictures good speech as carefully sifted and arranged, producing fellowship among those who hear it.
hinduism.tie_back: Speech sifted and ordered by the mind is the Kural’s nirantu, orderly speech that wins people over.
hinduism.source: Rigveda 10.71.2, trans. R. T. H. Griffith
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good on ordered speech; the hymn does not mention swift obedience.

christianity.quote_or_event: At Pentecost Peter gives a carefully built sermon, moving from prophecy to the resurrection to a call to repentance; the hearers are cut to the heart and about three thousand accept his word that same day.
christianity.explanation: Peter’s orderly argument produces an immediate and large response.
christianity.tie_back: Ordered speech followed by swift response is the pattern the Kural describes.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good narrative fit; Acts credits the Holy Spirit rather than rhetorical skill.

islam.quote_or_event: “Those are the ones of whom Allah knows what is in their hearts, so turn away from them but admonish them and speak to them a far-reaching word.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet is told to speak qawlan balīghan, an effective word that reaches deep into the hearers’ souls.
islam.tie_back: Speech that reaches and moves its hearers is the kind the Kural says people act on at once.
islam._accuracy_note: Fits the effectiveness theme; says nothing specific about order or quick obedience.

judaism.quote_or_event: Abigail meets David on his way to take revenge on her husband Nabal and makes a gracious, well-ordered plea; David at once blesses her good sense and turns back from bloodshed.
judaism.explanation: Her tactful, well-arranged speech changes an armed leader’s course on the spot.
judaism.tie_back: David’s immediate change of course shows the Kural’s point: orderly, pleasant speech gets swift results.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches the householder Upāli by a step-by-step talk (anupubbikathā) on generosity, virtue, heaven, the drawbacks of sensual pleasure and renunciation, then the Four Noble Truths, and Upāli gains the vision of the Dhamma where he sits.
buddhism.explanation: The Pali texts often show this graded, ordered discourse leading to immediate understanding in the listener.
buddhism.tie_back: A talk ordered step by step that brings instant acceptance matches the Kural’s swift response to orderly, sweet speech.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong fit on ordered speech bringing quick results.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says that when the Muses honour a king, they pour sweet dew on his tongue, so gentle words flow from his mouth; the people look to him as he settles disputes with straight judgements and quickly ends even a great quarrel.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Muses’ gift of sweet, well-formed speech lets a ruler bring the people along at once.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Sweet speech that quickly settles affairs and wins the people’s trust is the Kural’s image.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close, including the political setting; paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates says every speech should be put together like a living creature, with its own body, head and feet, and a middle and ends that fit each other and the whole.
philosophy.explanation: Plato makes well-ordered structure the mark of a speech worth hearing.
philosophy.tie_back: An organic, well-arranged speech is the Kural’s nirantu, orderly speech.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on order; says nothing about hearers’ swift response.

kurals.tamil:
பலசொல்லக் காமுறுவர் மன்றமா சற்ற
சிலசொல்லல் தேற்றா தவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Palasollak kaamuruvar mandramaa satra
Silasollal thetraa thavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who do not know how to say a few flawless words are surely the ones who love to say many.
kurals.elementary: Some people talk and talk because they can’t find the right few words. Someone who knows exactly what to say can say it quickly and clearly, like a good arrow that hits the target in one shot.
kurals.university: The couplet sets pala (many) against cila (few), and māc aṟṟa (stainless, faultless) qualifies the few words. Kāmuṟuvar, “they desire”, turns wordiness into a craving. Maṉṟa is an emphatic particle, “certainly, surely”, which Mu. Varadarasanar renders as uṇmaiyāka. Tēṟṟātavar means those who are not able or not skilled: Parimelazhagar takes it as inability to express a matter in few faultless words, so wordiness is a symptom of lacking the skill, not a separate vice. Pope’s rendering (“Who have not skill ten faultless words to utter plain”) adds a number not in the Tamil. In the older edition the second line reads சிலசொல்ல றேற்றா தவர், where sandhi turns collal tēṟṟā into colla ṟēṟṟā.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Sanskrit poet Śrīharṣa defines eloquence (vāgmitā) as speech that is measured and substantial (mitaṃ ca sāraṃ ca), a line that became a common saying.
hinduism.explanation: The epic poem Naiṣadhīyacarita places true eloquence in brief speech full of substance, not in many words.
hinduism.tie_back: Few words full of substance is the Kural’s ideal, and its opposite is the lover of many words.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close in idea; the verse number is from the standard citation and was not checked against an edition.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus rejects the idea that more words make speech more effective.
christianity.tie_back: Trusting in much speaking is the fault the Kural traces to lacking skill with a few good words.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good fit, though the context is prayer rather than counsel.

islam.quote_or_event: “The Prophet (ﷺ) used to talk so clearly that if somebody wanted to count the number of his words, he could do so.”
islam.explanation: Aisha describes the Prophet’s speech as measured and distinct, in contrast to someone who rushed through narrations.
islam.tie_back: Countable, deliberate words are the few faultless words the Kural praises.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on economy and clarity of speech.

judaism.quote_or_event: “all my days I grew up among the sages, and I have found nothing better for a person than silence. Study is not the most important thing, but actions; whoever indulges in too many words brings about sin.”
judaism.explanation: Shimon son of Rabban Gamaliel warns that many words lead to fault.
judaism.tie_back: Too many words bringing sin is the reverse of the Kural’s few flawless words.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on the danger of wordiness; Avot praises silence more than skill.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Better than a thousand useless words is one useful word, hearing which one attains peace.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada values one meaningful word above a flood of empty ones.
buddhism.tie_back: One useful word against a thousand useless ones is exactly the Kural’s few against many.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “the speech of Menelaus ran trippingly on the tongue; he did not say much, for he was a man of few words, but he spoke very clearly and to the point”
greek_mythology.explanation: Antenor remembers Menelaus as a speaker who used few words but made each count.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Menelaus is the Kural’s master of few, faultless words.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal ends one of his Provincial Letters by apologising that he made it longer than usual only because he had not had the time to make it shorter.
philosophy.explanation: Pascal’s joke makes the point that brevity takes more skill and effort than length.
philosophy.tie_back: Length as the fallback of one without time or skill is exactly the Kural’s diagnosis.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close in insight; paraphrased from the well-known postscript.

kurals.tamil:
இணருழ்த்தும் நாறா மலரனையர் கற்றது
உணர விரித்துரையா தார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Inaroozhththum naaraa malaranaiyar katradhu
Unara viriththuraiyaa thaar.
kurals.meaning: Those who cannot explain what they have learned so that others understand it are like flowers that bloom in clusters but give no fragrance.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a bunch of beautiful flowers that have no smell at all: nice to look at, but something is missing. A person who knows a lot but can’t explain it to anyone is like that. Learning is meant to be shared.
kurals.university: The closing couplet uses an uvamai (simile): iṇar (a cluster or bunch) ūḻttum (though it blossoms) nāṟā malar (a flower that gives no scent). Kaṟṟatu uṇara virittu uraiyātār means those who do not expand (virittu) and state (urai) what they have learned so that others may grasp it (uṇara). Parimelazhagar’s point is that learning (kalvi), however full, is incomplete in a counsellor unless it can be communicated, which links this chapter back to ch. 40 (Kalvi) and ch. 42 (Kēḷvi). The texts differ on the first word: ytamizh.com prints இணருழ்த்தும் with a short u, and the older edition prints இணருழ்த்து நாறா; many standard editions have the expected long-vowel form இணரூழ்த்தும் (iṇar + ūḻttum). The older edition also divides the second line as கற்ற / துணர விரித்துரையா தார் for metre.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Rigvedic hymn to Knowledge describes a man who has learned speech but whose speech is barren, bearing neither fruit nor flower, because he has abandoned the friend who shares knowledge.
hinduism.explanation: The hymn condemns learning that produces nothing for others, using the image of a flowerless, fruitless plant.
hinduism.tie_back: The Vedic image of speech without flower or fruit is very close to the Kural’s flower without fragrance.
hinduism.source: Rigveda 10.71.5-6, trans. R. T. H. Griffith
hinduism._accuracy_note: Striking parallel in both idea and plant imagery; paraphrased.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that light is meant to be seen and shared, not hidden.
christianity.tie_back: A candle under a bushel, like a scentless flower, is a good thing that fails to reach anyone else.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good fit on unshared goodness; the Gospel refers to witness and good works, not learning.

islam.quote_or_event: “And untie the knot from my tongue / That they may understand my speech.”
islam.explanation: Moses asks God to free his tongue so that his hearers can understand what he has been given to say.
islam.tie_back: Moses’ prayer is for the very skill the Kural requires: explaining what one knows so others grasp it.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close to uṇara virittu uraittal, speaking so others understand.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But Moses said to God, “Please, O my Sovereign, I have never been a man of words, either in times past or now that You have spoken to Your servant; I am slow of speech and slow of tongue.””
judaism.explanation: Moses, who has received God’s message, fears he cannot put it into words for Pharaoh and the people, so God appoints Aaron as his spokesman.
judaism.tie_back: Moses has the knowledge but fears he lacks the expression, the exact gap the Kural describes.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match; the Torah provides a solution (Aaron) instead of passing judgement.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like a beautiful flower full of color but without fragrance, even so, fruitless are the fair words of one who does not practice them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada uses the same image of a scentless flower for words that are not matched by practice.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts use the scentless flower, but the Kural applies it to unshared learning and the Dhammapada to unpractised words.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Identical image with a different target: the Kural faults learning that is not expressed, the Dhammapada words that are not practised.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Plutarch tells how the young Demosthenes, though learned and full of ideas, was jeered in the assembly for weak delivery, until the actor Satyrus showed him that the same words spoken with the right expression carried quite different force; he then trained himself into Athens’ greatest orator.
greek_mythology.explanation: The story shows knowledge without the power to convey it being ignored until the skill of expression is gained.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The young Demosthenes was the Kural’s scentless flower, full of learning but unable to reach his hearers.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good thematic fit, but this is Greek historical legend, not mythology.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his last speech in Thucydides, Pericles says that a man who knows what is right but cannot explain it clearly is no better off than if he had never thought of it at all.
philosophy.explanation: Pericles lists the ability to explain policy as a basic quality of a statesman, alongside knowing it.
philosophy.tie_back: Knowledge that cannot be expressed is worth no more than ignorance, which is the Kural’s scentless flower.
philosophy.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 2.60, trans. Richard Crawley
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match, also in the context of statecraft; paraphrased.
